methodology: Canonical Gospel/Acts and Old Testament references are primary for claims made by biblical authors. External archaeological, heritage and historical sources support only the independent material-history claims to which they are attached. Timelines show approximate periods, not a fully dated life of Jesus. Illustrative pins and outlines are NOT surveyed ancient borders, pilgrim routes or site footprints. This is research-based editorial synthesis, not peer-reviewed certification.
reviewStatus: Source-linked editorial research; external specialist review outstanding

cities.name: Jerusalem
cities.strapline: Temple, kingship, feasts and the final week
ancient: Zion (often poetic or part of the city)
cities.status: A securely located city, but not every Gospel event site can be fixed.
cities.lead: Jerusalem unites royal traditions, the Temple and Jesus' final days. The Gospel accounts place multiple visits and teachings here; archaeology provides evidence for the city's ancient settlement and its Second Temple urban setting without verifying every room, trial route or sacred spot.

timeline.description: The biblical histories depict David taking Jerusalem and making it a royal centre. Modern archaeological arguments about the scale and chronology of early Judah are debated.
Royal, religious and administrative Jerusalem is described in Kings and the prophets; remains in the City of David area document Iron Age habitation.

timeline.dates: Late first century BCE to first century CE
timeline.description: Herodian building and pilgrimage infrastructure shaped the city experienced by Jesus. Surviving excavated streets, steps, walls and residential areas document the setting, not individual miracles.
Roman destruction reshaped the city after the Gospel events. This later horizon is archaeologically distinct from the ministry years.
Churches and commemorative locations accumulated over later centuries, preserving traditions that are not identical to first-century archaeological proof.

findings.title: Herodian Upper City
findings.claim: Remains of substantial housing, walls and urban growth document Jerusalem in the late Second Temple period.
findings.limitation: The finds establish a city context, not where a specific Gospel conversation happened.

findings.title: Temple precinct approaches
findings.claim: Archaeological park remains include southern steps and entrances associated with pilgrimage access.
findings.limitation: The retained structures are not evidence that Jesus used a particular stone step.

findings.title: City of David and earlier layers
findings.claim: Multiple Iron Age and later remains attest occupation on the southeastern ridge.
findings.limitation: Attribution of individual walls and palaces to biblical figures is debated.

findings.title: Holy Sepulchre and sacred sites
findings.claim: Later Christian pilgrimage monuments commemorate the death and burial narratives.
findings.limitation: Cultural importance of commemoration does not independently prove a precise Gospel event spot.

debates: The exact locations of the trial settings, Golgotha and the burial tomb cannot all be confirmed archaeologically.
The Synoptic Gospels and John present different patterns of Jerusalem visits and temple action chronology.
Topography, streets and borders changed between the First Temple, Second Temple and later periods.

cities.name: Nazareth
cities.strapline: A Galilean home in an Early Roman village
cities.status: Early Roman settlement attested; no excavated house can be named Jesus' home.
cities.lead: The Gospels identify Nazareth as the community in which Jesus grew up and as the scene of a synagogue reading. Published excavations now provide material context for an Early Roman village, including domestic activity and subterranean storage spaces. Later pilgrimage sites should not be mistaken for excavated proof of a specific family dwelling.

timeline.dates: Tenth to early eighth centuries BCE
timeline.description: One excavated area preserves Iron Age occupation strata; this does not establish an OT narrative featuring Nazareth.

timeline.dates: Late second to first century BCE
timeline.description: Excavated strata indicate occupation before the period of Jesus.
Dwelling and silo/pit evidence supports an occupied Jewish settlement in the Gospel-era region.
Church and pilgrimage landscapes developed around traditional accounts of the Annunciation and Jesus' upbringing.
Modern archaeological projects reassess domestic structures and layers without identifying a secure Jesus-family household.

findings.title: Late Hellenistic / Early Roman strata

findings.limitation: Occupation evidence does not assign an excavated dwelling to Mary, Joseph or Jesus.

findings.limitation: The specific biblical household attribution is a later tradition, not a proven archaeological identity.

findings.title: Settlement as farming community
findings.claim: Site-wide work supports a first-century Galilean village with Jewish material culture.
findings.limitation: Population size and the boundaries of the Gospel-era settlement are not securely fixed.

findings.title: Annunciation traditions
findings.claim: Christian churches and local commemoration preserve later religious traditions tied to Nazareth.
findings.limitation: The Gospel narratives do not provide coordinates for these traditional holy sites.

debates: Nazareth is not named in the Old Testament; avoid treating later theological allusions as a named historical reference.
The Luke 4 synagogue scene is recorded at Nazareth, but no existing building is proven to be that synagogue.
Whether Mark 6 and Luke 4 report one visit or separate visits is a Gospel-harmonisation question.

cities.name: Capernaum
cities.strapline: Lakeside teaching, healings and a later monumental synagogue
cities.modern: Tell Hum, northwestern Sea of Galilee
cities.status: Roman-period settlement established; monumental limestone synagogue is later.
cities.lead: Capernaum is a recurring Gospel setting for Jesus' teaching and healings. Excavated basalt domestic remains supply a first-century village context, while the prominent white limestone synagogue belongs to a later construction phase. The distinction matters: an ancient town can be well identified without proving the exact room or building of any Gospel event.

timeline.description: Domestic occupation formed the community reflected by the Gospel references; basalt was a common local building stone.
Mark, Matthew, Luke and John place teaching, healings and household episodes here.
A house-site was adapted and commemorated in Christian architecture; its traditional association with Peter remains an identification of devotion.
The excavated limestone synagogue and earlier underlying structural levels are distinct archaeological phases.
Successive campaigns investigated the synagogue, domestic remains and later churches, revising earlier dating proposals.

findings.limitation: No individual miracle or occupant can be established from house walls alone.

findings.title: White limestone synagogue
findings.claim: Custody site investigations date the monumental limestone phase later than the first century, with underlying earlier constructions.
findings.limitation: The visible synagogue should not be labelled the unchanged building used by Jesus; dating arguments have a research history.

findings.title: Traditional Peter house
findings.claim: Christian memorial buildings were built over earlier domestic phases at a venerated house-site.
findings.limitation: The attribution of a specific dwelling to Simon Peter is not independently demonstrable.

findings.title: Synagogue inscriptions and architectural fragments
findings.claim: The excavation inventory records architectural ornament and inscriptions associated with later synagogue remains.
findings.limitation: Decoration reflects later worship architecture, not what the first-century synagogue necessarily looked like.

debates: The earlier synagogue beneath the visible later structure cannot simply be identified with the exact building Jesus entered.
Multiple visits to the same town may be narrative episodes rather than a count of separate journeys.
The town is secure enough for a city-level marker, while events within private houses are not pinpointed.

cities.name: Bethlehem
cities.strapline: Davidic traditions and the infancy narratives
cities.status: The town is identified; the Nativity grotto is a Christian traditional attribution.
cities.lead: Bethlehem links the David narratives and the infancy accounts of Jesus. Scripture names the town; centuries of Christian commemoration identify the Church of the Nativity and a grotto with the birthplace. UNESCO documents that history of belief and architecture, not a first-century archaeological demonstration of the birth location.

timeline.description: Ruth and Samuel describe Bethlehem in family, tribal and royal traditions.
Micah names Bethlehem Ephrathah in a prophecy associated with a ruler; Matthew cites this passage.

timeline.dates: Late first century BCE / early first century CE, dates debated
timeline.description: Luke and Matthew name Bethlehem but do not provide coordinates for the stable, building or grotto.
UNESCO records a Christian tradition of birthplace identification dating back to at least the second century.
An early church was completed by 339 CE; the current building largely reflects its sixth-century reconstruction and later changes.

findings.title: Church of the Nativity construction phases
findings.claim: UNESCO records fourth-century church construction and surviving sixth-century rebuilding with earlier floor elements.
findings.limitation: Monumental phases postdate Jesus by centuries; they document commemoration.

findings.title: Grotto identification
findings.claim: A site beneath the church has been honoured as Jesus' birthplace from early Christian centuries.
findings.limitation: The textual record does not identify this specific cave and archaeology cannot verify the birth event.

findings.title: Pilgrimage route and monastic complexes
findings.claim: Later pilgrimage routes, monasteries and churches document centuries of Christian veneration.
findings.limitation: These do not establish the path followed by Mary and Joseph or the magi.

findings.title: Davidic association
findings.claim: Ruth, Samuel and Micah situate the town within narratives and poetry concerning Davidic origins.
findings.limitation: Biblical literary claims remain distinct from archaeological proof of particular family households.

cities.name: Jericho
cities.strapline: Ancient oasis, conquest narrative and Gospel encounters
cities.modern: Jericho, West Bank and its environs
cities.status: The Bronze Age tell and Herodian-era palace landscape are distinct sites and time periods.
cities.lead: Jericho's long archaeological sequence predates New Testament events by millennia. The Bronze Age mound Tell es-Sultan supplies evidence for the ancient oasis, while the Hellenistic and Herodian palaces southwest of modern Jericho offer a more relevant picture of the late Second Temple period. The Gospels name Jericho for encounters with a blind man or men and Zacchaeus, without fixing the exact roadside or household.

timeline.dates: Around tenth to ninth millennia BCE
timeline.description: Tell es-Sultan preserves one of the region's earliest substantial settled communities, including a Neolithic tower and walls.
Successive city phases include defensive constructions and urban occupation visible in excavated tell layers.
Joshua, Kings and the Elisha narratives connect Jericho with Israelite history in texts spanning different horizons.
The southwest oasis royal-palace remains document elite occupation and gardens in the wider district near the Gospel era.
The Gospels report healing a blind person or persons and meeting Zacchaeus in or near Jericho. Their accounts vary about approach/departure.

findings.title: Tell es-Sultan stratigraphy
findings.claim: UNESCO records numerous archaeological occupation phases with Neolithic and Bronze Age structures.
findings.limitation: These surviving earlier walls cannot on their own establish the specific event in Joshua 6.

findings.title: Neolithic tower and settlement
findings.claim: A stone tower, walls and early settled occupation are well documented at the ancient tell.
findings.limitation: This material is several millennia earlier than the Gospel scenes.

findings.title: Herodian-era palace landscape
findings.claim: Palace remains at Tulul Abu el-Alayiq southwest of Jericho illustrate Herodian elite presence and the late Hellenistic-Roman oasis.
findings.limitation: The UNESCO entry is a tentative-list description, not World Heritage inscription or proof of Zacchaeus' house.

findings.title: Location of Zacchaeus' home
findings.claim: Luke records Jesus entering Jericho and visiting Zacchaeus.
findings.limitation: A tourist-labelled sycamore or dwelling cannot be verified as the specific tree or home from Luke 19.

debates: The archaeological chronology of Bronze Age Jericho and interpretation of Joshua 6 must not be collapsed into a simplistic statement of confirmation or disproof.
Mark, Matthew and Luke differ on approach/departure and number of blind people; our itinerary notes these variants.
The ancient tell, Herodian palace estates and Gospel-era town are related but not interchangeable locations.
